[[Category:Gradient descent]]
[[Category:Artificial neural network]]

'''Stochastic gradient descent''' (SGD) is a variant of [[gradient descent]] that optimises computation for aggregated differentiable objective function by estimating the gradient from a random sample of the data at each iteration. 

It is the standard algorithm used to train [[artificial neural network (ANN)]] models on large datasets.

== Mathematical definition ==

Let

$$
f=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{k \in I} f_k
$$

then

$$
\vec x_{i+1} = \vec x_i - \frac{\eta}{|I_1|}\sum_{k \in I_1 \subset I} \nabla f_k(\vec x_i),
$$

where $I_1 \subset I$ is the sample examined at iteration $i$. The step uses the average sampled gradient rather than its sum, so that $\eta$ keeps the same meaning whatever the sample size.

== Validity ==

[[File:Gradient descrent classic v.png|thumbnail|Classic (left) v. stochastic (right) gradient descent. Classic descent is like an old and wise person taking careful small steps directly towards the goal, while stochastic descent is like a young drunkard stumbling rapidly in the general direction.]]
The true gradient is the average of the per-datapoint gradients,

$$
\nabla f(\vec x_i)
=
\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{k \in I}\nabla f_k(\vec x_i),
$$

and the stochastic estimate must therefore also be an average rather than a sum. That is what the factor $1/|I_1|$ is: the sample size, dividing the sum over the sampled datapoints by how many terms that sum contains.

Without the factor the estimate is biased, because the sample holds only $|I_1|$ of the $|I|$ terms. Each datapoint is equally likely to be drawn, $\mathbb{P}(k \in I_1)=|I_1|/|I|$, so taking the expectation over the draw of $I_1$ with $\vec x_i$ fixed,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k \in I_1 \subset I}\nabla f_k(\vec x_i)\right]
=
\sum_{k \in I}\mathbb{P}(k \in I_1)\nabla f_k(\vec x_i)
=
\frac{|I_1|}{|I|}\sum_{k \in I}\nabla f_k(\vec x_i)
=
|I_1|\,\nabla f(\vec x_i).
$$

The raw sample sum therefore overshoots the true gradient by the factor $|I_1|$. Dividing by $|I_1|$ cancels that factor exactly,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|I_1|}\sum_{k \in I_1 \subset I}\nabla f_k(\vec x_i)\right]
=
\nabla f(\vec x_i),
$$

so the expected value of the sample gradient equals the true gradient. Therefore, the stochastic gradient is an unbiased estimator of the true gradient, whatever the sample size.

== Advantage ==

=== In training [[artificial neural network (ANN)]] ===

Training large ANNs require large datasets with millions of datapoints and thousands of iterations. Calculating the true gradient requires evaluating $f_k$ for each datapoint, which is computationally prohibitive. Stochastic gradient descent significantly reduces computation burden without sacrificing accuracy.
